questions.prompt: A script that creates a storage bucket is run twice. What property would stop it creating a second bucket?
choices: Idempotency: it compares what exists with what is wanted and only acts on the difference
questions.explanation: Infrastructure as code is a reconciler. The engine reads current state, diffs it against the desired configuration, and applies only the delta, so repeating a run with no changes does nothing.

questions.prompt: Why does the engine keep a state file at all, when it could just look at the disk?
choices: To know which real resources it owns and what their last-applied attributes were, so it can tell its own resources from everything else and detect drift
questions.explanation: The provider can read a file, but it cannot know whether that file was created by this configuration. State is the mapping from resource address to real-world id, plus the last attributes applied.

questions.prompt: You change a `local_file`'s `path`. Why does the plan show `-/+` (replace) instead of `~` (update)?
choices: path is an immutable attribute: the provider cannot move the resource in place, so it must destroy and create
questions.explanation: Each provider declares which attributes force replacement. In Terraform you see this as `# forces replacement` next to the attribute; it is the most common source of accidental data loss.

questions.prompt: Someone deletes a managed file by hand. What does the next plan show after refresh?
choices: A create, because the resource is in state but missing in reality (drift)
questions.explanation: Refresh reads reality into the plan. The desired configuration still wants the file, state says it existed, reality says it does not, so the plan recreates it.

questions.prompt: In a real Terraform or OpenTofu plan, which line deserves a second look before approving in CI?
choices: Any `-` or `-/+` on a database, bucket or volume, because destroy means data loss
questions.explanation: Creates and in-place updates are usually safe. Destroys and replacements of stateful resources are where outages come from; `prevent_destroy` and plan review gates exist for exactly this.

questions.prompt: Two engineers run apply at the same time against the same state file. What is the failure mode and the fix?
choices: Nothing happens; the second run waits
Both read the old state, both act, the second write overwrites the first: lost updates and duplicated resources. Fix: a state lock and remote state
questions.explanation: State is a shared record. Terraform backends lock it (DynamoDB, S3 lockfile, Postgres advisory locks) so only one plan/apply can run; the Hard exercise adds the same to minitf.
